assumptions: That the ZeroDivisionError is caused by dividing by a zero-valued denominator (e.g. an empty period or zero-count spend) is inferred from the exception type and file/line only; the source of src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:32 was not read.

That the defect pre-dates the flag flip rests on the absence of deploys in the change channel across every window queried (roughly 2026-09-03 onward, and one query spanning ~31 days). Absence of recorded deploys is not proof that none occurred — it may also mean the change feed does not cover this service.

The mitigation's failure is attributed to the flag being on again rather than to the fix being wrong. This is inferred from flag-evaluation log lines reading `on` through 14:27 and a recorded toggle to `on` at 14:26:32; who or what performed that toggle (the provider, a human, or Argus's own action failing and being re-applied) was not determined.

The flag provider history was read three times and reported only one recent flag change each time, which is inconsistent with an off-then-on sequence around 14:23-14:26. Either the provider history is stale/deduplicated or Argus's revert never reached the provider; this was not resolved and weakens confidence in both the revert and its refutation.

The incident end timestamp of 14:28:05 coincides exactly with escalation to humans, not with any observed return to baseline. No log line or metric after 14:27 shows recovery, so the true duration of customer impact is unknown and may extend past the recorded end.
The ~1-3% background error rate before 14:18 is a separate, pre-existing UpstreamTimeout condition on payment authorization, assumed unrelated to this incident and left uninvestigated.
Impact is assumed limited to account-page requests, because every error line in the window names the account page. Downstream or retry effects on other flows were not checked.

Several investigator queries requested log windows extending past the current time (e.g. the 19 minutes before 14:45 at 14:27), which returned only a handful of lines; some duplicated log blocks in the record are re-reads of the same minutes rather than distinct events.
input.executive_summary: Starting at 14:18 UTC on 17 September 2026, a portion of customers loading their account page received an error instead of the page. The cause was a new spending-summary feature that was switched on for customers that minute; the code behind it failed whenever it tried to calculate an average over a customer with no spending activity. Nothing had been newly released — the fault was existing code that only became reachable once the feature was turned on. Other parts of the shop, such as browsing and checkout, were not implicated; the failures were confined to the account page. Automated response picked the incident up within a second of the alert and correctly identified the new feature as the trigger within fifteen seconds. It turned the feature off at 14:23, but the feature was recorded as switched back on three minutes later and the system's own records show it never running in the off state, so the automation concluded its fix had not worked and kept searching. At 14:28, after re-examining the evidence and reaching the same conclusion, it handed the incident to on-call engineers. The whole automated phase lasted about five minutes from alert to escalation. The impact figure for this incident is taken from what the shop actually recorded, not from any estimate made here.
input.root_cause: The feature flag `monthly-spend-feature` was switched on at 14:18 (partial that minute, fully on from 14:19), which routed account-page traffic into a code path that raises `ZeroDivisionError` at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:32; account-page requests that hit that path failed immediately. The defect was pre-existing and dormant — no deploy or release appears anywhere in the change record read for io-shop — so the flag flip was the trigger and the unguarded division the fault. Mitigation was attempted (flag reverted at 14:23:28) but the flag evaluation logs read `on` continuously from 14:19 through 14:27, including after a toggle back to `on` at 14:26:32, so the service was never observed running with the flag off and the correct hypothesis was wrongly marked refuted; the incident was escalated to humans at 14:28 with the defect still exposed.
